title: Erdos Problem #101: Four-Point Lines from Planar Point Sets
description: Given n points in the plane with no five collinear, is the number of lines containing exactly four points o(n^2)? Grunbaum showed the count can be at least n^{3/2}. Solymosi-Stojakovic achieved n^{2-O(1/sqrt(log n))}, disproving Erdos's Theta(n^{3/2}) conjecture. The o(n^2) upper bound remains open ($100).

references: Erdos (1984): original conjecture in 'Problems and results in combinatorial geometry'
Grunbaum: construction achieving n^{3/2} four-point lines
Solymosi-Stojakovic (2013): n^{2-O(1/sqrt(log n))} lower bound construction
Szemeredi-Trotter (1983): 'Extremal problems in discrete geometry' incidence bound
Burr-Grunbaum-Sloane: collinear triples without four-point lines

sections.title: Header and Imports
sections.summary: Module docstring stating the problem, its status as OPEN with $100 prize, and Mathlib imports for finsets, naturals, and tactics.

sections.title: Core Definitions
sections.summary: Defines PlanarPointSet as a nonempty finite subset of R^2, collinearity via the signed area determinant test, the NoFiveCollinear condition quantifying over all 5-element subsets, and fourPointLineCount counting collinear 4-subsets via powerset filtering.
sections.mathContext: Key definitions: $P \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with $|P| > 0$; collinear$(p,q,r)$ iff signed area vanishes; $f_4(P) = |\{S \in \binom{P}{4} : S$ collinear$\}|$.

sections.title: Main Conjecture
sections.summary: The central open problem: the four-point line count is o(n^2), formalized as an epsilon-N_0 statement. For any epsilon > 0, sufficiently large no-five-collinear sets have fewer than epsilon * n^2 four-point lines.
sections.mathContext: $\forall \varepsilon > 0,\, \exists N_0$ such that $f_4(P) < \varepsilon |P|^2$ for all no-five-collinear $P$ with $|P| \geq N_0$.

sections.title: Known Lower and Upper Bounds
sections.summary: Three key bounds: Grunbaum's n^{3/2} lower bound construction, Solymosi-Stojakovic's nearly quadratic n^{2-O(1/sqrt(log n))} improvement that disproved the Theta(n^{3/2}) conjecture, and the trivial O(n^2) upper bound from line counting.
sections.mathContext: $\Omega(n^{3/2}) \leq f_4^{\max}(n) \leq O(n^2)$, with Solymosi-Stojakovic achieving $n^{2 - O(1/\sqrt{\log n})}$.

sections.title: Related Results and Tools
sections.summary: Two complementary results: Burr-Grunbaum-Sloane/Furedi-Palasti constructions of sets with n^2/6 collinear triples but zero four-point lines, and the Szemeredi-Trotter incidence theorem O(n^{2/3}m^{2/3} + n + m) as the fundamental bounding tool.

overview.historicalContext: Erdos posed this problem in his 1984 paper 'Problems and results in combinatorial geometry,' asking whether the maximum number of four-point lines determined by n points with no five collinear is o(n^2). He initially conjectured the answer is Theta(n^{3/2}), based on Grunbaum's lattice-based construction achieving that many four-point lines. The problem connects to a rich tradition in discrete geometry going back to Sylvester's 1893 question about ordinary lines. In 2013, Solymosi and Stojakovic dramatically disproved the Theta(n^{3/2}) conjecture by constructing configurations with n^{2-O(1/sqrt(log n))} four-point lines -- nearly quadratic, leaving only a subpolynomial gap to the trivial O(n^2) upper bound. The o(n^2) question itself remains one of the most important open problems in combinatorial geometry, with a $100 Erdos prize attached. It sits at the intersection of incidence geometry, algebraic methods (polynomial partitioning), and extremal combinatorics.
overview.problemStatement: Given $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with no five collinear, prove that the number of lines containing exactly four of the points is $o(n^2)$.
overview.proofStrategy: We formalize the point-set configuration as a structure PlanarPointSet with a nonemptiness invariant, define collinearity via the standard signed-area determinant, and express the no-five-collinear condition by quantifying over all 5-element subsets. The four-point line count is defined by filtering the powerset for collinear 4-subsets. The main conjecture and all known bounds (Grunbaum's lower bound, Solymosi-Stojakovic's improvement, the trivial upper bound) are stated as axioms, along with the Szemeredi-Trotter incidence bound as the key tool from the area.
keyInsights: The no-five-collinear threshold is sharp: allowing five collinear points trivially yields Omega(n^2) four-point lines by placing points on two lines
Grunbaum's n^{3/2} construction uses lattice points on algebraic curves to create many collinear quadruples while controlling five-point collinearities
Solymosi and Stojakovic's nearly quadratic construction reveals that the gap between lower and upper bounds is subpolynomial, making the o(n^2) conjecture much more delicate than originally expected
The Szemeredi-Trotter incidence theorem provides the key constraint: if m lines are each 4-rich (contain >= 4 points), then 4m <= I(P,L) <= O(n^{2/3}m^{2/3} + n + m), giving m = O(n^2) but not o(n^2)
The existence of configurations with ~n^2/6 collinear triples but zero four-point lines (Burr-Grunbaum-Sloane) shows a fundamental discontinuity between 3-collinear and 4-collinear behavior
Related Erdos problems #102 (collinear quadruples), #588 (k-rich lines), and #669 (ordinary lines) form a family of collinearity problems with deep interconnections

conclusion.summary: This formalization captures one of the central open problems in combinatorial geometry: whether the maximum number of four-point lines from n points (no five collinear) is o(n^2). The Theta(n^{3/2}) conjecture by Erdos was dramatically disproved by Solymosi and Stojakovic's nearly quadratic construction, but the o(n^2) bound itself remains stubbornly open, with a $100 Erdos prize still unclaimed.
conclusion.implications: A resolution would have far-reaching consequences for discrete geometry. A proof of the o(n^2) bound would require fundamentally new techniques beyond Szemeredi-Trotter, potentially involving polynomial partitioning or algebraic methods. Conversely, a disproof (constructing Omega(n^2) four-point lines with no five collinear) would resolve one of the few remaining $100 Erdos problems and reshape our understanding of collinearity extremals.
openQuestions: Is the four-point line count truly o(n^2), or can one construct Omega(n^2) four-point lines with no five collinear?
Can the Solymosi-Stojakovic construction be improved to Omega(n^2 / polylog(n)), closing the gap further?
Does polynomial partitioning (Guth-Katz style) yield progress on the upper bound side?
What is the situation in higher dimensions -- does the analogous question for hyperplanes have a different answer?
Is there a connection to the Erdos unit distance problem or the distinct distances problem via similar incidence-geometric tools?
